invalid_if: A reporting window is used to defeat a statutory consumer right
A consumer refusing defective goods is charged for delivery
name: Failed and Refused Delivery
title: Failed Delivery
text:
Where a delivery cannot be completed, the following applies.
(a) {{company_name}} shall attempt delivery at least {{delivery_attempts}} times, and shall inform the consumer before each attempt by the contact details given with the order.
(b) Where delivery cannot be completed after those attempts, the order is returned to {{company_name}} and the amount paid is refunded in accordance with the Refund and Cancellation Policy.
(c) A consumer who refuses delivery of goods that are damaged, defective, or not as described shall receive a full refund, including any delivery charge paid.
(d) Where goods are delivered short, damaged, or in a tampered package, the consumer should report it through the platform within {{shortage_report_days}} days of delivery, and {{company_name}} shall investigate and, where the report is made out, replace the goods or refund the amount paid.
(e) Failure to report within that period does not by itself extinguish a right the consumer has under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

legal_basis.note: Duties of e-commerce entities in relation to delivery and shipment

source: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020; Consumer Protection Act, 2019; Sale of Goods Act, 1930
statutory_reference: Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 - R.4; Consumer Protection Act, 2019 - S.2(11)
authoring_note: Limb (e) exists because a short reporting window is often drafted as a condition precedent to any remedy. It is not: the statutory rights subsist, and a clause purporting to extinguish them by the passage of a few days is an unfair contract term. The advocate should set the reporting window.
